planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Firespire's narrow columnar form makes it a good street tree or tight-space substitute for the wide-spreading species.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Firespire was selected from a block of seedling American hornbeams for its unusually tight, narrow, upright habit and is sold under this trademark name. Unlike the broad, rounded, multi-stemmed form typical of straight-species Carpinus caroliniana, Firespire grows as a dense column reaching roughly 20-25 feet tall but only 8-15 feet wide, making it useful for narrow side yards, street tree strips, and formal allees where the native musclewood would otherwise be too wide. It retains the smooth, sinewy, blue-gray bark that gives the species its musclewood and ironwood nicknames, and its glossy dark green summer foliage turns a consistently brilliant orange-red in autumn, brighter and more reliable than most seedling-grown trees. Like the species it is exceptionally shade tolerant and adaptable to wet or dry soils once established, and it makes a durable small specimen or screening tree in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast landscapes where its narrow footprint is an asset.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; site beneath taller canopy trees as an understory specimen.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally beneath the high canopy of larger deciduous trees; Rosea is an old, long-cultivated selection of Carolina silverbell prized for producing flowers in shades of pink rather than the pure white of the species. Bloom color is somewhat weather-dependent, with cooler spring temperatures producing deeper rose-pink bells and warmer springs yielding a paler blush pink, but the dangling, four-petaled, bell-shaped flowers always appear in dense clusters along bare branches in April before the leaves fully emerge. In every other respect Rosea behaves like the species: a graceful small understory tree to 30 feet with a similar spread, moderately fast growth, and a preference for the same moist ravines and shaded stream banks where wild silverbells are found from the Appalachians down into the Gulf Coastal Plain. It can be slow to establish and resents root disturbance, so it should be planted from containers rather than transplanted bare-root, and it benefits from a site sheltered from strong wind and drying afternoon sun.
sources: Dirr, M.A. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained-to-boggy soil in full sun to partial shade; Moonglow tolerates wetter sites than most magnolias, making it useful near ponds, ditches, and low areas.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Moonglow, registered under the cultivar name Jim Wilson, is a vigorous, upright-growing selection of sweetbay magnolia noted for large, deep green semi-evergreen leaves and improved cold hardiness that keeps foliage on the tree through winters as cold as -28F. Like the species, it produces creamy white, lemon-scented, cup-shaped flowers that open intermittently from late spring through summer rather than in one concentrated flush, giving a much longer bloom season than most magnolias. Sweetbay magnolia is naturally found in wet pine flatwoods, bay swamps, and pond margins across the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains, and Moonglow retains that tolerance for poorly drained, seasonally saturated soils where few other flowering trees perform. It grows as a broad, rounded, multi-stemmed or single-trunk tree reaching 35-40 feet tall, larger and looser in habit than some of the more compact sweetbay selections, and it is an excellent choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and low spots in Gulf Coast landscapes.
sources: conservation district native plant fact sheets

common_name: Green Shadow Sweetbay Magnolia (Fully Evergreen Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained-to-wet soil in full sun to light shade; the tight oval habit and reliably evergreen foliage suit it to screening and specimen use.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Green Shadow was selected from seedlings for staying fully evergreen through severe winters that defoliate ordinary sweetbay magnolias, retaining its glossy, dark green, silvery-backed leaves after exposure to temperatures near -20F, a significant improvement over typical seed-grown sweetbays that drop their leaves once cold sets in. The tree forms a tighter, more upright oval than the loose, multi-stemmed habit of the species, reaching about 25-30 feet tall and 20 feet wide, and produces the same fragrant, creamy-white, globe-shaped flowers from late spring into summer. As with all sweetbay magnolias it is naturally adapted to wet, boggy, acidic soils of pine flatwoods and pond margins across the coastal plain, making Green Shadow a strong choice for a year-round screen or specimen tree in consistently moist Gulf Coast garden soils.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root plants in late winter to early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; site as an understory shrub or hummingbird-garden specimen.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; splendens is a long-recognized selection of the native red buckeye distinguished by its exceptionally intense, glossy scarlet-red flower panicles, showier and darker in color than the more common orange-red to salmon-toned wild forms of the species. It grows as a large, rounded, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree to about 12-15 feet, one of the earliest woody plants to leaf out and bloom in the Gulf Coast spring, producing upright clusters of tubular red flowers in April that are a critical early nectar source for migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds. Like the species, it is native to rich woodlands, river bluffs, and shaded ravine slopes from the Carolinas to Texas, and it goes summer-dormant after a hard July drought, dropping its leaves early without harm to the plant. This form is propagated by grafting or cuttings to preserve its superior flower color, since seedling red buckeyes are variable and often paler.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; give it ample room since it suckers and spreads into a large colony over time.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial to full shade; Rogers was selected and named from the naturally later-blooming, larger-flowered variety of bottlebrush buckeye known as var. serotina, and it remains the best-known named cultivar of that variety in general cultivation. It blooms two to three weeks later than the typical species, opening its flower spikes in mid-to-late July rather than June, and those upright, bottlebrush-shaped flower panicles are considerably longer, up to 30 inches, than the 6-12 inch panicles of straight-species Aesculus parviflora. Over time it forms a large, dense, suckering, multi-stemmed colony that can reach 12-20 feet tall and equally wide, making it one of the best large-scale flowering shrubs for heavy shade, useful as a woodland-edge mass planting or shade-garden anchor where its late, extended bloom period is especially valuable after most other spring shrubs have finished. It tolerates full shade better than almost any other flowering shrub but is intolerant of dry soils, particularly while young.

common_name: Autumn Gold Bald Cypress (Improved Fall-Color Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; tolerates standing water as well as ordinary well-drained landscape soil once established.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; Autumn Gold is a selection of bald cypress bred for a dense, fine-textured, uniformly pyramidal habit with a single dominant central leader, correcting the more irregular, open branching often seen in seedling-grown trees. Its main horticultural advantage is fall color: the needle-like foliage turns a consistent, rich rusty-orange to gold in autumn, showier and more reliable across a planting than straight-species bald cypress, which can vary from tan to orange to almost no color at all. Like the species, it is superbly adapted to the swamps, riverbanks, and seasonally flooded bottomlands of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains, tolerating both permanent standing water and, once established, average well-drained upland soil, and it develops the flared, buttressed trunk base typical of the species with age. Growing 50-70 feet tall and 20-30 feet wide at maturity, Autumn Gold makes an excellent uniform street tree, pond-edge specimen, or avenue planting where a predictable narrow-pyramidal form and dependable fall color are priorities.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart for a continuous evergreen screen or hedge.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Viburnum x pragense arose in Prague in the 1950s as a hybrid between leatherleaf viburnum (V. rhytidophyllum) and V. utile, combining the bold, deeply veined, glossy dark-green evergreen foliage of the former parent with a tighter, more refined habit and greater cold hardiness than either parent alone. In early spring it produces flat-topped clusters of small, lightly fragrant white flowers opening from pink buds, followed by red fruit that ripens to black, though fruit set is generally sparse. It grows at a fast rate into a dense, upright-oval shrub 8-12 feet tall and equally wide, making it one of the most reliable broadleaf evergreen viburnums for creating a year-round privacy screen or informal hedge. The corrugated, felted-underside leaves give useful textural contrast next to smoother-leaved evergreens.
sources: Oregon State University Landscape Plants database
